sources.text: Google Cloud revenues increased $15.5 billion from 2024 to 2025, primarily driven by growth in Google Cloud Platform largely from infrastructure and platform services.

Google Cloud operating income increased $7.8 billion from 2024 to 2025. The increase in operating income was primarily driven by an increase in revenues, partially offset by increases in usage costs for technical infrastructure and employee compensation expenses.

Google Cloud revenues consist of revenues from:

- Google Cloud Platform primarily generates consumption-based fees and subscriptions for infrastructure, platform, and other services. These services provide access to solutions such as AI offerings including our enterprise AI infrastructure, Vertex AI platform, and Gemini Enterprise; cybersecurity offerings; and data and analytics solutions;

- Google Workspace includes subscriptions for cloud-based communication and collaboration tools for enterprises, such as Gmail, Docs, Calendar, Drive, and Meet, with integrated features like Gemini for Google Workspace; and

- other enterprise services.

Google Cloud revenues are comprised of the following:

- Google Cloud Platform primarily generates consumption-based fees and subscriptions for infrastructure, platform, and other services. These services provide access to solutions such as AI offerings including our enterprise AI infrastructure, Vertex AI platform, and Gemini Enterprise; cybersecurity offerings; and data and analytics solutions;

- Google Workspace includes subscriptions for cloud-based communication and collaboration tools for enterprises, such as Gmail, Docs, Calendar, Drive, and Meet, with integrated features like Gemini for Google Workspace; and

- other enterprise services.

Fluctuations in our Google Cloud revenues have been, and may continue to be, affected by factors in addition to the general factors described above, such as changes in customer usage, demand, and supply availability.

(1)    For additional information on the calculation of diluted net income per share, see Note 12 of the Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements included in Item 8 of this Annual Report on Form 10-K.

- Revenues were $402.8 billion, an increase of 15% year over year, primarily driven by an increase in Google Services revenues of $37.8 billion, or 12%, and an increase in Google Cloud revenues of $15.5 billion, or 36%.

- Cost of revenues was $162.5 billion, an increase of 11% y  ear over year, primarily driven by increases in TAC, content acquisition costs, and depreciation expense.

-  Operating exp  enses were $111.3 billion, an increase of 22% ye  ar over year, primarily driven by increases in employee compensation expenses, e  xpenses related to legal and other matters, and depreciation expense.

Google Search & other revenues increased $26.4 billion from 2024 to 2025. Google Search & other revenues increased $26.4 billion from 2024 to 2025. ## YouTube ads

YouTube ads revenues increased $4.2 billion from 2024 to 2025. The growth was driven by our direct response advertising products followed by our brand advertising products, both of which benefited from increased spending by our advertisers.

## Google Network

Google Network revenues decreased $567 million from 2024 to 2025, primarily due to a decrease in AdSense revenues, partially offset by an increase in AdMob revenues.

Microsoft's Intelligent Cloud revenue in fiscal year 2024 was **$87.5 billion** ($87,464 million) under the current segment definitions, or **$105.4 billion** ($105,362 million) as originally reported in the FY2024 10-K.

- **Restated (current) basis — $87.5 billion:** In August 2024 Microsoft changed its segment composition, most notably moving the commercial components of Microsoft 365 into Productivity and Business Processes, and recast prior periods. The FY2025 10-K reports FY2024 Intelligent Cloud revenue of $87,464 million on this basis, which is also what the database holds.
- **As originally reported — $105.4 billion:** The FY2024 10-K (old segment definitions) reported Intelligent Cloud revenue of $105,362 million for FY2024, up 20% from $87,907 million in FY2023, driven by Azure and other cloud services (which grew 30%).
- Under the restated basis, Intelligent Cloud was Microsoft's second-largest segment in FY2024, behind Productivity and Business Processes ($106.8 billion) and ahead of More Personal Computing ($50.8 billion); total FY2024 revenue was $245.1 billion on both bases.

sources.section: Fiscal Year 2025 Compared with Fiscal Year 2024
sources.text:
Revenue increased $36.6 billion or 15% with growth across each of our segments. Intelligent Cloud revenue increased driven by Azure. Productivity and Business Processes revenue increased driven by Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud. More Personal Computing revenue increased driven by Gaming and Search and news advertising.

Cost of revenue increased $13.7 billion or 19% driven by growth in Microsoft Cloud.

Gross margin increased $22.9 billion or 13% with growth across each of our segments.

- Gross margin percentage decreased slightly driven by Intelligent Cloud, offset in part by More Personal Computing.

- Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage decreased to 69% driven by the impact of scaling our AI infrastructure, offset in part by efficiency gains in Azure.

Our Microsoft Cloud revenue, which includes Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud, Azure and other cloud services, the commercial portion of LinkedIn, and Dynamics 365, was $168.9 billion, $137.7 billion, and $111.6 billion in fiscal years 2025, 2024, and 2023, respectively. These amounts are included in Microsoft 365 Commercial products and cloud services, Server products and cloud services, LinkedIn, and Dynamics products and cloud services in the table above.

Assets are not allocated to segments for internal reporting presentations. A portion of amortization and depreciation is included with various other costs in an overhead allocation to each segment. It is impracticable for us to separately identify the amount of amortization and depreciation by segment that is included in the measure of segment profit or loss.

We report our financial performance based on the following segments: Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing. The segment amounts included in MD&A are presented on a basis consistent with our internal management reporting.

In August 2024, we announced changes to the composition of our segments. These changes align our segments with how we currently manage our business, most notably bringing the commercial components of Microsoft 365 together in the Productivity and Business Processes segment. Beginning in fiscal year 2025, the information that our chief operating decision maker is regularly provided and reviews for purposes of allocating resources and assessing performance reflects these segment changes. Prior period segment information has been recast to conform to the way we internally manage and monitor our business during fiscal year 2025.

result.answer:
Microsoft's FY2025 10-K defines Microsoft Cloud revenue as revenue from Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud, Azure and other cloud services, the commercial portion of LinkedIn, and Dynamics 365 — and it was $168.9 billion in FY2025, $137.7 billion in FY2024, and $111.6 billion in FY2023.

- **Definition (MD&A, Item 7):** "Microsoft Cloud revenue and revenue growth — Revenue from Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud, Azure and other cloud services, the commercial portion of LinkedIn, and Dynamics 365." The segment note in Item 8 repeats this: "Our Microsoft Cloud revenue, which includes Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud, Azure and other cloud services, the commercial portion of LinkedIn, and Dynamics 365."
- **Amounts (Item 8, segment note):** $168.9 billion (FY2025), $137.7 billion (FY2024), and $111.6 billion (FY2023). The MD&A highlights that Microsoft Cloud revenue increased 23% in FY2025 versus FY2024.
- **Where it sits in reported revenue:** the filing notes these amounts are included within the Microsoft 365 Commercial products and cloud services, Server products and cloud services, LinkedIn, and Dynamics products and cloud services lines of the product-and-service revenue table (e.g., FY2025: $87.8 billion, $98.4 billion, $17.8 billion, and $7.8 billion, respectively). Microsoft Cloud is thus a cross-segment measure, not one of the three reportable segments.
- Microsoft Cloud revenue is a filing-only figure; it is not in the structured database, which holds only the three reportable segments (Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, More Personal Computing).

Sources: [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.80], [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.36], [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.33]

Our Microsoft Cloud revenue, which includes Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud, Azure and other cloud services, the commercial portion of LinkedIn, and Dynamics 365, was $168.9 billion, $137.7 billion, and $111.6 billion in fiscal years 2025, 2024, and 2023, respectively. These amounts are included in Microsoft 365 Commercial products and cloud services, Server products and cloud services, LinkedIn, and Dynamics products and cloud services in the table above.

Assets are not allocated to segments for internal reporting presentations. A portion of amortization and depreciation is included with various other costs in an overhead allocation to each segment. It is impracticable for us to separately identify the amount of amortization and depreciation by segment that is included in the measure of segment profit or loss.

We generate revenue by offering a wide range of cloud-based solutions, content, and other services to people and businesses; licensing and supporting an array of software products; delivering relevant online advertising to a global audience; and designing and selling devices. Our most significant expenses are related to compensating employees; supporting and investing in our cloud-based services, including datacenter operations; designing, manufacturing, marketing, and selling our other products and services; and income taxes.

Highlights from fiscal year 2025 compared with fiscal year 2024 included:

- Microsoft Cloud revenue increased 23% to $168.9 billion.

- Microsoft 365 Commercial products and cloud services revenue increased 14% driven by Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud revenue growth of 15%.

Apple's net income fell by **$3.3 billion (3.4%)**, from $97.0 billion in FY2023 to $93.7 billion in FY2024, despite revenue growing 2.0% to $391.0 billion — and the 10-K attributes the decline to a one-time income tax charge related to the European Commission State Aid Decision.

- **The numbers:** Net income fell from $96,995 million to $93,736 million (−$3,259 million, −3.4%), while revenue rose from $383,285 million to $391,035 million (+2.0%). Operating income actually *grew* 7.8% to $123,216 million, so the decline came below the operating line.
- **The cause per the 10-K:** On September 10, 2024, the European Court of Justice set aside the 2020 General Court judgment and confirmed the Commission's 2016 State Aid Decision. As a result, in Q4 2024 Apple recorded a **one-time income tax charge of $10.2 billion, net** — $15.8 billion payable to Ireland via release of escrow, partially offset by a $4.8 billion U.S. foreign tax credit and an $823 million decrease in unrecognized tax benefits.
- **Tax impact:** The provision for income taxes rose from $16,741 million in 2023 to $29,749 million in 2024 (an increase of $13.0 billion), and the effective tax rate jumped from 14.7% to 24.1%. The MD&A states the 2024 effective tax rate was higher than 2023 "due primarily to a one-time income tax charge of $10.2 billion, net, related to the State Aid Decision," along with a higher effective tax rate on foreign earnings and lower tax benefits from share-based compensation.
- The underlying obligation stems from the Commission's 2016 decision that Ireland granted Apple state aid through 1991 and 2007 tax opinions, with a recovery amount of €13.1 billion plus €1.2 billion interest for the period June 2003 through December 2014.

sources.text:
The Company’s effective tax rate for 2024 was higher than the statutory federal income tax rate due primarily to a one-time income tax charge of $10.2 billion, net, related to the State Aid Decision (refer to Note 7, “Income Taxes” in the Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements in Part II, Item 8 of this Form 10-K) and state income taxes, partially offset by a lower effective tax rate on foreign earnings, the impact of the U.S. federal R&D credit, and tax benefits from share-based compensation.

The Company’s effective tax rate for 2024 was higher compared to 2023 due primarily to a one-time income tax charge of $10.2 billion, net, related to the State Aid Decision, a higher effective tax rate on foreign earnings and lower tax benefits from sharebased compensation.

The Company and Ireland appealed the State Aid Decision to the General Court of the Court of Justice of the European Union (the “General Court”). On July 15, 2020, the General Court annulled the State Aid Decision. On September 25, 2020, the Commission appealed the General Court’s decision to the European Court of Justice (the “ECJ”) and a hearing was held on May 23, 2023. On September 10, 2024, the ECJ announced that it had set aside the 2020 judgment of the General Court and confirmed the Commission’s 2016 State Aid Decision. As a result, during the fourth quarter of 2024 the Company recorded a one-time income tax charge of $10.2 billion, net, which represents $15.8 billion payable to Ireland via release of the escrow, partially offset by a U.S. foreign tax credit of $4.8 billion and a decrease in unrecognized tax benefits of $823 million.

On August 30, 2016, the Commission announced its decision that Ireland granted state aid to the Company by providing tax opinions in 1991 and 2007 concerning the tax allocation of profits of the Irish branches of two subsidiaries of the Company (the “State Aid Decision”). The State Aid Decision ordered Ireland to calculate and recover additional taxes from the Company for the period June 2003 through December 2014. Irish legislative changes, effective as of January 2015, eliminated the application of the tax opinions from that date forward. The recovery amount was calculated to be €13.1 billion, plus interest of €1.2 billion.

As of September 28, 2024, the Company had an obligation to pay €14.2 billion or $15.8 billion to Ireland in connection with the State Aid Decision, all of which was expected to be paid within 12 months. The funds necessary to settle the obligation were held in escrow as of September 28, 2024, and restricted from general use.

result.answer:
Apple spent more: Apple repurchased $89.3 billion of its common stock in fiscal 2025, versus $45.4 billion for Alphabet — a difference of $43.9 billion (Apple's spend was 1.97 times Alphabet's).

- **Apple (FY2025, ended September 27, 2025):** repurchased 402 million shares for $89.3 billion. It used the final $19.8 billion of its May 2024 $110 billion program in Q4, and announced a new $100 billion program on May 1, 2025, of which $221 million had been utilized by fiscal year-end.
- **Alphabet (FY2025, ended December 31, 2025):** repurchased and retired 240 million shares for $45.4 billion — $6.5 billion of Class A shares (37 million shares) and $38.9 billion of Class C shares (203 million shares). Its Board authorized $70.0 billion programs in both April 2024 and April 2025, with $69.5 billion remaining available as of December 31, 2025.
- Note the fiscal years cover different calendar months (Apple's ended in late September 2025; Alphabet's ended December 31, 2025).

Sources: [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.27 and p.45], [GOOGL FY2025 10-K, p.42 and p.80]

Our repurchase program does not have an expiration date and does not obligate Alphabet to repurchase any specific dollar amount or to acquire any specific number of shares. Our cash dividend program pays regular cash dividends to our Class A, Class B, and Class C stockholders. Any and all future cash dividends are subject to declaration by our Board of Directors in its sole discretion, and in accordance with the requirements of any applicable laws, rules, and regulations, including the Delaware General Corporation Law. Our cash dividend program does not require, and our Board of Directors may decide not to declare, a cash dividend each quarter, and does not obligate our Board of Directors to declare a dividend at any specific dollar amount per share. Any such decision by our Board of Directors may depend on a variety of factors that it may deem relevant, including but not limited to our earnings, liquidity, financial condition, other capital deployment opportunities, level of indebtedness, and general market conditions. Our share repurchases and dividends could affect our share trading prices, increase their volatility, reduce our cash reserves and may be suspended or terminated at any time, which may result in a decrease in the trading prices of our stock.

Microsoft Cloud accounted for approximately 60.0% of Microsoft's fiscal year 2025 total revenue ($168.9 billion of $281.7 billion).

- Microsoft Cloud revenue was $168.9 billion in FY2025, up 23% from $137.7 billion in FY2024, per the FY2025 10-K.

- Microsoft Cloud includes Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud, Azure and other cloud services, the commercial portion of LinkedIn, and Dynamics 365; these amounts are included within the Microsoft 365 Commercial, Server products and cloud services, LinkedIn, and Dynamics product lines in the 10-K's revenue table.
- Note that Microsoft Cloud is a product/service grouping, not one of Microsoft's three reportable segments (Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, More Personal Computing).

sources.text:
We generate revenue by offering a wide range of cloud-based solutions, content, and other services to people and businesses; licensing and supporting an array of software products; delivering relevant online advertising to a global audience; and designing and selling devices. Our most significant expenses are related to compensating employees; supporting and investing in our cloud-based services, including datacenter operations; designing, manufacturing, marketing, and selling our other products and services; and income taxes.

Highlights from fiscal year 2025 compared with fiscal year 2024 included:

- Microsoft Cloud revenue increased 23% to $168.9 billion.

- Microsoft 365 Commercial products and cloud services revenue increased 14% driven by Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud revenue growth of 15%.

Our Microsoft Cloud revenue, which includes Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud, Azure and other cloud services, the commercial portion of LinkedIn, and Dynamics 365, was $168.9 billion, $137.7 billion, and $111.6 billion in fiscal years 2025, 2024, and 2023, respectively. These amounts are included in Microsoft 365 Commercial products and cloud services, Server products and cloud services, LinkedIn, and Dynamics products and cloud services in the table above.

Assets are not allocated to segments for internal reporting presentations. A portion of amortization and depreciation is included with various other costs in an overhead allocation to each segment. It is impracticable for us to separately identify the amount of amortization and depreciation by segment that is included in the measure of segment profit or loss.

**Alphabet (GOOGL) spent the largest share of revenue on R&D in FY2025 — 15.2% ($61.1 billion of R&D on $402.8 billion of revenue)** — ahead of Microsoft at 11.5% ($32.5 billion on $281.7 billion) and Apple at 8.3% ($34.6 billion on $416.2 billion). (Note: fiscal years differ — Alphabet's ends December 31, 2025; Microsoft's June 30, 2025; Apple's late September 2025.)

What Alphabet's FY2025 10-K says about its AI infrastructure investment:

- **Trend disclosure (MD&A, "Increased Investment in Technical Infrastructure"):** Alphabet says it continues to invest in capital expenditures as it scales its technical infrastructure, "in particular for AI," to meet demand from users and enterprise customers and to support internal research. It invested heavily in capex in 2025 and expects to **significantly increase** its investment in 2026 relative to 2025, including servers and network equipment and data centers.
- **Capex figures:** Capital expenditures were **$91.4 billion in 2025, up from $52.5 billion in 2024** (a 74.1% increase), primarily reflecting investments in technical infrastructure. Depreciation on property and equipment rose to $21.1 billion from $15.3 billion.
- **Rising operating costs:** The costs of operating its technical infrastructure — depreciation, energy, equipment, and network capacity — are expected to significantly increase because developing and serving AI offerings "require more compute power than our historical consumer and enterprise offerings." It expects to keep driving data-center efficiencies, for example through the design of its AI models and its TPU- and GPU-based infrastructure.
- **Strategic framing (Item 1):** Alphabet describes its AI-optimized infrastructure as "a key differentiator" at the foundation of its full-stack approach, powering its own products (Search, YouTube) and Google Cloud, with a range of AI accelerators including specialized GPUs and its custom-built TPUs, such as Ironwood, its seventh-generation TPU. Per the financial statements, approximately 60% of technical infrastructure assets consist of servers and network equipment.

sources.section: Trends in Our Business and Financial Effect
sources.text: **_Increased Investment in Technical Infrastructure:_** We continue to invest in capital expenditures as we scale our technical infrastructure, in particular for AI, to meet the demand of our users and enterprise customers and to support research internally. We invested heavily in capital expenditures in 2025 and in 2026, we expect to significantly increase  , relative to 2025, our in  vestment in our technical infrastructure, including servers and network equipment, and data centers. The costs associated with operating our technical infrastructure - depreciation, energy, equipment, and network capacity - are expected to significantly increase as developing and serving AI offerings require more compute power than our historical consumer and enterprise offerings. While our technical infrastructure costs increase, we expect to continue to drive efficiencies in our data centers, for example, through the design of our AI models and our TPU and GPU-based technical infrastructure.

Our capital investments in property and equipment consist primarily of the following major categories:

- technical infrastructure, which consists of our investments in servers and network equipment, data center land, and building construction and improvements; and

- office facilities, ground-up development projects, and building improvements.

Assets not yet in service are those that are not ready for their intended use, including assets in the process of construction or assembly, and consist primarily of technical infrastructure. The time frame from date of purchase to placement in service of these assets may extend from months to years. For example, our data center construction projects are generally multi-year projects with multiple phases, where we acquire land and buildings, construct buildings, and secure and install servers and network equipment.

During the years ended December 31, 2024 and 2025, we spent $52.5 billion and $91.4 billion on capital expenditures, respectively. In 2026, we expect to significantly increase  , relative to 2025, our in  vestment in our technical infrastructure, including servers and network equipment, and data centers. Depreciation of our property and equipment commences when such assets are ready for their intended use. For the years ended December 31, 2024 and 2025, our depreciation on property and equipment was $15.3 billion and $21.1 billion, respectively.

At the foundation of our full-stack approach is our AI-optimized infrastructure — a key differentiator enabling us to power our own products, such as Search and YouTube, and support the services we provide to our Google Cloud customers. Our technical infrastructure allows us to use and offer our customers a range of AI accelerator options, including specialized Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) and our own custom-built Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), such as Ironwood, our seventh-generation TPU. We are focused on driving efficiencies in our data centers, allowing us to leverage our technical infrastructure to deliver our products and services at an increasing scale while simultaneously enabling world-class research and model development.

- Operating cash flow was $164.7 billion for the year ended December 31, 2025.

- Capital expenditures, which primarily reflected investments in technical infrastructure, were $91.4 billion for the year ended December 31, 2025.

- As of  December 31, 2025, we had  190,820 employees.

We are monitoring ongoing developments surrounding international trade and the macroeconomic environment. As a result of volatility in international trade and financial markets, we may experience direct and indirect effects on our business, operations, and financial results. Our past results may not be indicative of our future performance, and our financial results may differ materially from historical trends.

sources.section: We face intense competition. If we do not continue to innovate and provide products and services that are useful to users, customers, and other partners, we may not remain competitive, which could harm our business, financial condition, and operating results.
sources.text: Our business environment is rapidly evolving and intensely competitive. Our businesses face changing technologies, shifting user needs, and frequent introductions of rival products and services. To compete successfully, we must accurately anticipate technology developments and deliver innovative, relevant, and useful products, services, and technologies in a timely manner. For example, with the rise of AI in recent years, we have increasingly focused our investments in building powerful AI tools and AI enhancements to our existing products and services to better cater to our users, customers, and other partners. As our businesses evolve, the competitive pressure to innovate will encompass a wider range of products and services. We must continue to invest significant resources in technical infrastructure, including the development of our custom TPUs, and research and development, including through acquisitions, in order to enhance our technology, products, and services.

Through our Google Cloud Platform and Google Workspace offerings, Google Cloud generates revenues primarily from consumption-based fees and subscriptions for infrastructure, platform, applications, and other cloud services. Customers use Google Cloud in multiple ways such as:

- **AI-optimized Infrastructure:** runs on our Cloud, at the edge, or in customers' data centers. It can be used to migrate and modernize information technology (IT) systems and to train and serve various types of AI models. Our AI infrastructure delivers cost-performance for AI workloads. We offer a range of AI accelerators, including our custom TPUs and specialized GPUs, as well as AI-optimized storage offerings, and efficient AI software.

> (1) As of December 31, 2024 and 2025, approximately 60% of technical infrastructure assets were comprised of servers and network equipment. The remaining balance was comprised of data center land and buildings and related assets.

**_Making AI Helpful for Everyone_**

We believe AI is a profound platform shift that can bring meaningful and positive change to people and societies across the world, and to our business. We aim to build the most advanced, safe, and responsible AI through our fullstack approach, which spans AI-optimized infrastructure; world-class research, including models and tooling; and our products and platforms that bring AI to billions of people, developers, and enterprises.

Greater China was Apple's worst-performing geographic segment in fiscal 2025 — the only one of the five reportable segments whose net sales declined, and the 10-K attributes the decrease primarily to lower iPhone sales.

- **Net sales fell 3.8%**, from $66,952 million in FY2024 to $64,377 million in FY2025, a decline of $2,575 million. Every other segment grew: Americas +7% ($178,353M), Europe +10% ($111,032M), Japan +15% ($28,703M), and Rest of Asia Pacific +10% ($33,696M).
- **Reason given in the 10-K (MD&A, Segment Operating Performance):** "Greater China net sales decreased during 2025 compared to 2024 primarily due to lower net sales of iPhone, partially offset by higher net sales of Mac."
- Segment operating income also slipped, from $27,082 million in FY2024 to $26,917 million in FY2025 (Note 13, Segment Information and Geographic Data).
- This was the second consecutive annual decline for Greater China: net sales were $72,559 million in FY2023, down 8% in FY2024 and another 4% in FY2025.

Microsoft's operating income grew $19.1 billion (+17.4%) and Alphabet's grew $16.6 billion (+14.8%) in their respective fiscal 2025 years (Microsoft's FY2025 ended June 30, 2025; Alphabet's ended December 31, 2025).

**Microsoft** — operating income rose from $109.4 billion to $128.5 billion. The FY2025 10-K says the $19.1 billion (17%) increase came "with growth across each of our segments":
- Revenue increased $36.6 billion or 15%: Intelligent Cloud driven by Azure (Azure and other cloud services revenue grew 34%), Productivity and Business Processes driven by Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud, and More Personal Computing driven by Gaming and Search and news advertising.
- Gross margin increased $22.9 billion or 13%, while operating expenses rose only $3.8 billion or 6% (investments in cloud and AI engineering and Gaming, including the Activision Blizzard acquisition impact).
- By segment: Productivity and Business Processes operating income +$10.1 billion (17%), Intelligent Cloud +$6.8 billion (18%), More Personal Computing +$2.2 billion (18%). The filing notes gross margin percentage decreased slightly from scaling AI infrastructure, offset in part by efficiency gains in Azure and Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud.

**Alphabet** — operating income rose from $112.4 billion to $129.0 billion. The FY2025 10-K attributes the increase to its two Google segments, partly offset by losses elsewhere:
- Google Services operating income +$18.1 billion, "primarily driven by an increase in revenues, partially offset by an increase in expenses related to legal and other matters, TAC, and content acquisition costs."
- Google Cloud operating income +$7.8 billion, "primarily driven by an increase in revenues, partially offset by increases in usage costs for technical infrastructure and employee compensation expenses" (Cloud revenue rose $15.5 billion to $58.7 billion).
- These gains were partially offset by a $3.1 billion wider Other Bets operating loss (employee compensation, largely a valuation-based compensation charge related to Waymo) and a $6.2 billion wider Alphabet-level activities loss, which the filing says primarily reflects expenses for shared AI research and development.

**Microsoft grew operating income the fastest from FY2024 to FY2025, at 17.4%** (from $109.4 billion to $128.5 billion), ahead of Alphabet at 14.8% ($112.4B → $129.0B) and Apple at 8.0% ($123.2B → $133.1B).

**Growth rates (FY2024 → FY2025):**
- Microsoft: +17.4% ($109,433M → $128,528M)
- Alphabet: +14.8% ($112,390M → $129,039M)
- Apple: +8.0% ($123,216M → $133,050M)

**What Microsoft's FY2025 10-K says drove the growth (operating income up $19.1 billion or 17%, "with growth across each of our segments"):**
- **Revenue up $36.6 billion or 15%**, with Intelligent Cloud driven by Azure, Productivity and Business Processes driven by Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud, and More Personal Computing driven by Gaming and Search and news advertising. Microsoft Cloud revenue increased 23% to $168.9 billion.
- **Gross margin up $22.9 billion or 13%** with growth across each segment, more than covering a $13.7 billion (19%) rise in cost of revenue driven by growth in Microsoft Cloud. Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage decreased to 69% due to scaling AI infrastructure, offset in part by efficiency gains in Azure.
- **Operating expenses rose only $3.8 billion or 6%**, driven by investments in cloud and AI engineering and Gaming (including the Activision Blizzard acquisition) — so revenue/gross margin growth outpaced expense growth.
- **By segment:** Productivity and Business Processes operating income +$10.1 billion or 17% (gross margin driven by Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud, which grew 15%); Intelligent Cloud +$6.8 billion or 18% (Azure and other cloud services revenue grew 34%); More Personal Computing +$2.2 billion or 18% (Gaming revenue +9% on Xbox content and services, and Search and news advertising revenue ex-TAC +20% on higher search volume and revenue per search).

Note: fiscal years are not calendar-aligned — Microsoft's FY2025 ended June 30, 2025, Apple's ended late September 2025, and Alphabet's ended December 31, 2025.

Yes — all four rows in the database's `segment_revenue` table for Alphabet FY2025 sum exactly to its total revenue of $402.8 billion, but the three actual segments alone do not; the difference is a reconciling "Hedging gains (losses)" row of -$127 million.

- Database rows for GOOGL FY2025: Google Services $342.7 billion, Google Cloud $58.7 billion, Other Bets $1.5 billion, and Hedging gains (losses) -$127 million.
- Sum of all four rows: $402,836,000,000, which equals the FY2025 total revenue in `income_statements` ($402.8 billion) exactly.
- Sum of the three reportable segments only (Google Services + Google Cloud + Other Bets): $402,963,000,000 — $127 million above total revenue.
- The difference is the hedging line: the FY2025 10-K (Note 15, Information about Segments and Geographic Areas) reports the same figures and shows "Hedging gains (losses)" of $(127) million as a separate line between the segments and "Total revenues" of $402,836 million. Alphabet's reportable segments are only Google Services, Google Cloud, and Other Bets; the hedging gains (losses) row is a reconciling item, not a segment, so it must be included to tie to consolidated revenue.

Japan grew the fastest, with net sales up 14.6%, from $25.05 billion in FY2024 to $28.70 billion in FY2025. The FY2025 10-K attributes the increase primarily to higher net sales of iPhone, Services and iPad.

For context, the other regions' growth rates were: Rest of Asia Pacific +9.9%, Europe +9.6%, Americas +6.8%, while Greater China declined 3.8%.

Sources: [SQL: geographic_revenue], [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.24]

sources.sql:
SELECT region,
       MAX(CASE WHEN fiscal_year = 2024 THEN revenue END) AS fy2024,
       MAX(CASE WHEN fiscal_year = 2025 THEN revenue END) AS fy2025,
       ROUND((MAX(CASE WHEN fiscal_year = 2025 THEN revenue END) - MAX(CASE WHEN fiscal_year = 2024 THEN revenue END)) * 100.0 / MAX(CASE WHEN fiscal_year = 2024 THEN revenue END), 1) AS growth_pct
FROM geographic_revenue
WHERE company_ticker = 'AAPL' AND period_type = 'FY' AND fiscal_year IN (2024, 2025)
GROUP BY region
ORDER BY growth_pct DESC

Mac net sales increased during 2025 compared to 2024 primarily due to higher net sales of laptops and desktops.

Alphabet had the highest capital expenditures in FY2025 at $91.4 billion, while Microsoft had the highest capex relative to revenue at 22.9% of revenue.

- **Absolute capex (FY2025):** Alphabet $91.4 billion (purchases of property and equipment, year ended Dec 31, 2025) > Microsoft $64.6 billion (additions to property and equipment, year ended June 30, 2025) > Apple $12.7 billion (payments for acquisition of property, plant and equipment, year ended Sept 27, 2025).
- **Capex as a share of FY2025 revenue:** Microsoft 22.9% ($64.6B / $281.7B), Alphabet 22.7% ($91.4B / $402.8B), Apple 3.1% ($12.7B / $416.2B). Microsoft and Alphabet are close, but Microsoft's ratio is higher.
- Alphabet's MD&A attributes its capex primarily to investments in technical infrastructure (servers, network equipment, data center land and construction), and states it expects to significantly increase that investment in 2026. Microsoft's MD&A says it will continue to invest in capital expenditures to support growth in cloud offerings and AI infrastructure, and discloses $32.1 billion committed for construction of new buildings and improvements, primarily related to datacenters, as of June 30, 2025.
- Note the fiscal years cover different calendar months: Apple's FY2025 ended September 27, 2025, Microsoft's ended June 30, 2025, and Alphabet's ended December 31, 2025.

result.answer:
Both companies' FY2025 10-Ks say AI infrastructure spending is raising costs and pressuring margins: Microsoft states the investments "will continue to increase our operating costs and may decrease our operating margins," while Alphabet says its technical-infrastructure costs (depreciation, energy, equipment, network capacity) "are expected to significantly increase" because AI offerings require more compute power than historical offerings. (Note: Microsoft's FY2025 ended June 30, 2025; Alphabet's ended December 31, 2025.)

**Microsoft (FY2025 10-K)**
- MD&A "Economic Conditions, Challenges, and Risks" (p.34): investments in cloud and AI infrastructure and devices will continue to increase operating costs and may decrease operating margins; Microsoft continues to expand datacenter locations and server capacity "particularly given the growing demand for AI services," and depends on permitted land, predictable energy, networking supplies, and servers including GPUs. The Risk Factors section (p.17) similarly states Microsoft is "incurring significant costs to build and maintain infrastructure to support cloud-based and AI services, reducing operating margins."
- Realized effect in FY2025 (p.37–38): cost of revenue rose $13.7 billion or 19% driven by growth in Microsoft Cloud; gross margin percentage "decreased slightly driven by Intelligent Cloud"; Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage fell to 69% "driven by the impact of scaling our AI infrastructure, offset in part by efficiency gains in Azure." In Intelligent Cloud, cost of revenue rose $10.6 billion or 36% driven by Azure, with gross margin percentage down for the same reason.
- Quantified from the database: gross margin fell from 69.8% to 68.8% year over year, while operating margin actually rose from 44.6% to 45.6% (operating income up $19.1 billion to $128.5 billion on revenue up 15%).

**Alphabet (FY2025 10-K)**
- MD&A "Trends in Our Business and Financial Effect" (p.30): Alphabet invested heavily in capital expenditures in 2025 and expects to significantly increase investment in 2026 in servers, network equipment, and data centers; operating costs of that infrastructure — depreciation, energy, equipment, and network capacity — are expected to significantly increase because AI offerings require more compute power. It expects to offset this partly by "driv[ing] efficiencies in our data centers, for example, through the design of our AI models and our TPU and GPU-based technical infrastructure."
- Realized effect in FY2025 (p.34, 37): cost of revenues rose $16.2 billion or 11% to $162.5 billion, driven by TAC, content acquisition costs, and depreciation expense; the increase in other cost of revenues was "primarily due to increases in content acquisition costs, largely for YouTube, depreciation expense, and other technical infrastructure operations costs." Operating expenses also rose 22%, partly on depreciation expense.
- Quantified: operating margin was flat at 32% in both 2024 and 2025 (32.1% vs. 32.0% calculated), and cost of revenues as a percentage of revenues actually improved from 42% to 40% per the filing. The Risk Factors section (p.12) frames the margin risk as forward-looking: downward pressure on operating margin from "a higher level of investment in technical infrastructure," relatively fixed costs, and possible inability to keep driving efficiencies at the historical rate, plus mix shift toward lower-margin businesses such as Google Cloud.

In short, both filings describe AI infrastructure as a cost and margin headwind, but Microsoft attributes an actual FY2025 gross-margin decline to "scaling our AI infrastructure" (partly offset by Azure efficiency gains), while Alphabet reports flat operating margins for 2025 and frames the significant cost increases as expected going into 2026.

Sources: [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.34], [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.37], [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.38], [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.17], [GOOGL FY2025 10-K, p.30], [GOOGL FY2025 10-K, p.34], [GOOGL FY2025 10-K, p.37], [GOOGL FY2025 10-K, p.12], [SQL: income_statements]

sources.text: The investments we are making in cloud and AI infrastructure and devices will continue to increase our operating costs and may decrease our operating margins. We continue to identify and evaluate opportunities to expand our datacenter locations and increase our server capacity to meet the evolving needs of our customers, particularly given the growing demand for AI services. Our datacenters depend on the availability of permitted and buildable land, predictable energy, networking supplies, and servers, including graphics processing units (“GPUs”) and other components. Our devices are primarily manufactured by third-party contract manufacturers. For the majority of our products, we have the ability to use other manufacturers if a current vendor becomes unavailable or unable to meet our requirements. However, some of our products contain certain components for which there are very few qualified suppliers. Extended disruptions at these suppliers could impact our ability to manufacture devices on time to meet consumer demand.

- LinkedIn revenue increased $1.4 billion or 9% with growth across all lines of business.

- Dynamics products and cloud services revenue increased $996 million or 15% driven by growth in Dynamics 365, offset in part by a decline in Dynamics on-premises products. Dynamics 365 revenue grew 19% with growth across all workloads.

Operating income increased $10.1 billion or 17%.

- Cost of revenue increased $2.8 billion or 14% driven by growth in Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud.

sources.text:
Revenue increased $36.6 billion or 15% with growth across each of our segments. Intelligent Cloud revenue increased driven by Azure. Productivity and Business Processes revenue increased driven by Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud. More Personal Computing revenue increased driven by Gaming and Search and news advertising.

Cost of revenue increased $13.7 billion or 19% driven by growth in Microsoft Cloud.

Gross margin increased $22.9 billion or 13% with growth across each of our segments.

- Gross margin percentage decreased slightly driven by Intelligent Cloud, offset in part by More Personal Computing.

- Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage decreased to 69% driven by the impact of scaling our AI infrastructure, offset in part by efficiency gains in Azure.

**Our focus on cloud-based and AI services presents execution and competitive risks.** We are incurring significant costs to build and maintain infrastructure to support cloud-based and AI services, reducing operating margins. Whether we succeed in cloud-based and AI services depends on our execution in several areas, including:

- Continuing to bring to market compelling cloud-based and AI services and products that generate increasing traffic and market share.

- Maintaining the utility, compatibility, and performance of our cloud-based and AI services on the growing array of computing devices, including PCs, smartphones, tablets, gaming consoles, and other devices.

- Continuing to enhance the attractiveness of our cloud platforms to third-party developers.

- Server products and cloud services revenue increased $18.6 billion or 23% driven by Azure and other cloud services. Azure and other cloud services revenue grew 34% driven by demand for our portfolio of services. Server products revenue decreased 3% driven by a decrease in transactional purchasing with continued customer shift to cloud offerings.

- Enterprise and partner services revenue increased $166 million or 2% driven by growth in Enterprise Support Services, offset in part by a decline in Industry Solutions.

Operating income increased $6.8 billion or 18%.

- Cost of revenue increased $10.6 billion or 36% driven by growth in Azure.

- Gross margin increased $8.2 billion or 14% driven by growth in Azure. Gross margin percentage decreased driven by the impact of scaling our AI infrastructure, offset in part by efficiency gains in Azure.

sources.section: RISKS RELATING TO THE EVOLUTION OF OUR BUSINESS
sources.text: **We make significant investments in products and services that may not achieve expected returns.** We will continue to make significant investments in research, development, and marketing for existing products, services, and technologies, including AI-based products and services. We also invest in the development and acquisition of a variety of hardware for productivity, communication, and entertainment, including PCs, tablets, and gaming devices. Investments in new technology are speculative. Commercial success depends on many factors, including innovation, developer support, and effective distribution and marketing. If customers do not perceive our latest offerings as providing significant new functionality or other value, they may reduce their purchases of new software and hardware products or upgrades, unfavorably affecting revenue. We may not achieve significant revenue from new product, service, and distribution channel investments for several years, if at all. New products and services may not be profitable or may not achieve operating margins as high as we have experienced historically. We may not get engagement in certain features that drive post-sale monetization opportunities. Our data-handling practices across our products and services will continue to be under scrutiny. Perceptions of mismanagement, driven by regulatory activity or negative public reaction to our practices or product experiences, could negatively impact product and feature adoption. Developing new technologies is complex. It can require long development and testing periods. We could experience significant delays in new releases or significant problems in creating new products or services. These factors could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

sources.section: Trends in Our Business and Financial Effect
sources.text: **_Increased Investment in Technical Infrastructure:_** We continue to invest in capital expenditures as we scale our technical infrastructure, in particular for AI, to meet the demand of our users and enterprise customers and to support research internally. We invested heavily in capital expenditures in 2025 and in 2026, we expect to significantly increase  , relative to 2025, our in  vestment in our technical infrastructure, including servers and network equipment, and data centers. The costs associated with operating our technical infrastructure - depreciation, energy, equipment, and network capacity - are expected to significantly increase as developing and serving AI offerings require more compute power than our historical consumer and enterprise offerings. While our technical infrastructure costs increase, we expect to continue to drive efficiencies in our data centers, for example, through the design of our AI models and our TPU and GPU-based technical infrastructure.

sources.text: We may experience downward pressure on our operating margin resulting from a variety of factors. These include increasing costs for many aspects of our business resulting from a higher level of investment in technical infrastructure, increasing regulations, and increasing competition. Certain of our costs and expenses are relatively fixed and may not correlate to changes in revenue, and we may also not be able to continue to drive efficiencies at the rate we have in the past. We may also face margin compression from an increase in the mix of lower-margin products and services, in particular from the continued expansion of our business into new fields, including products and services such as Google Cloud, our devices, and consumer subscription products, as well as significant investments in Other Bets. For instance, margins on our devices have had, and may continue to have, an adverse effect on our consolidated margins due to pricing pressures and higher cost of sales. Due to these factors and the evolving nature of our business, our historical revenue growth rate and historical operating margin may not be indicative of our future performance.
